question_text:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of worsening fever, headache, photophobia, and nausea for 2 days. One week ago, she returned from summer camp. She has received all age-appropriate immunizations. Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F). She is oriented to person, place, and time. Physical examination shows a maculopapular rash. There is rigidity of the neck; forced flexion of the neck results in involuntary flexion of the knees and hips. Cerebrospinal fluid studies show:
Opening pressure 120 mm H2O
Appearance Clear
Protein 47 mg/dL
Glucose 68 mg/dL
White cell count 280/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 15%
Lymphocytes 85%
Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?"?

                    ### Question
                    A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of worsening fever, headache, photophobia, and nausea for 2 days. One week ago, she returned from summer camp. She has received all age-appropriate immunizations. Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F). She is oriented to person, place, and time. Physical examination shows a maculopapular rash. There is rigidity of the neck; forced flexion of the neck results in involuntary flexion of the knees and hips. Cerebrospinal fluid studies show:
Opening pressure 120 mm H2O
Appearance Clear
Protein 47 mg/dL
Glucose 68 mg/dL
White cell count 280/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 15%
Lymphocytes 85%
Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?"?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Echovirus
opb. Listeria monocytogenes
opc. Herpes simplex virus
opd. Streptococcus pneumoniae
ope. Neisseria meningitidis

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 13-year-old girl, including fever, headache, photophobia, nausea, neck rigidity, and a maculopapular rash, suggests viral meningitis. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows elevated white blood cell count with a predominance of lymphocytes (85%), which is characteristic of viral infections. The presence of a recent summer camp exposure raises the suspicion for common viral pathogens. Echovirus is a well-known cause of viral meningitis in children and is more prevalent in this context compared to Herpes simplex virus, which is less common in this age group. Bacterial meningitis is less likely due to the lymphocytic predominance in the CSF, and Listeria monocytogenes typically affects older adults. Therefore, the most likely causal organism is Echovirus.
